rounds.proof_sketch: Input shape is fixed at [128, 1], so size = 128. With block_size = 256, num_blocks = ceil(128/256) = 1. With a 1-block grid, blockIdx.x = blockIdx.y = 0 always. Original: idx = 0*256 + threadIdx.x. Mutated: idx = 0*256 + threadIdx.x. Both are identical.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes blockIdx.x to blockIdx.y in the index calculation. However, the kernel is launched with a 1D grid configuration <<<num_blocks, block_size>>>. With the fixed input shape [128, 1], the total size is 128 elements. Since block_size=256 and num_blocks = ceil(128/256) = 1, only a single block is launched. In a single-block 1D grid, both blockIdx.x and blockIdx.y are always 0 (gridDim is effectively (1,1,1)). Therefore, the mutation has no observable effect - both the original and mutated expressions evaluate to threadIdx.x. The Layer 2 evidence confirms bitwise equivalence across all 112 test rounds.
rounds.kill_strategy: UNKILLABLE under fixed-shape contract. The mutation would only be distinguishable if more than one block were launched (requiring size > 256), but the fixed input shape [128, 1] guarantees size=128, which always results in exactly 1 block where blockIdx.x = blockIdx.y = 0.
rounds.recommendations: When testing CUDA kernel mutations involving block/thread indices, verify whether the fixed input dimensions result in enough blocks to exercise multi-block behavior. This mutant would be killable with larger input sizes (>256 elements), suggesting mutation testing should consider boundary conditions around block sizes.
